title: The Quiet House
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: She came back to the house on a Tuesday in October, twelve years after her mother had died in it. The house had been closed since. Her father had never gone in. The paint should have been faded, the garden overgrown. Instead, the house was exactly as she remembered it. And in the bathroom, on the small shelf above the sink, were three toothbrushes.

chapters.title: Three Toothbrushes
chapters.body:
She came back to the house on a Tuesday in October, twelve years after her mother had died in it.

Her name was Sara Aaltonen. She was thirty-four. She had grown up in the house — a small wooden house in a small quiet neighborhood in the eastern part of Turku, on a street lined with birches that had, when she was a child, seemed enormous and now, on the taxi ride from the airport, seemed only ordinary — and she had left it at eighteen to go to university in Helsinki, and had, over the following years, come back less and less. Her mother had died in the house when Sara was twenty-two. The house had, since then, sat empty. Sara's father, who lived in an apartment in Tampere, had not been able to bring himself to sell it, and had not been able to bring himself to enter it, and had, in the twelve years since, maintained it at a distance — a woman came twice a year to clean, a plumber came each autumn to drain the pipes for the winter, the grass in the small garden was cut by a neighbor's son.

Sara's father had, in the previous month, been diagnosed with the same disease that had killed her mother. He had, on the telephone the week before, asked her to go to the house. He had asked her, in the small careful tired voice he had used for the last twelve years whenever the house came up, to sort what needed to be sorted, and to decide what needed to be decided, and to prepare it for sale.

She had said yes.

She had flown from Munich, where she now lived with her partner Ismo, on the Monday evening. She had spent the night in a small hotel near the market square. She had, on the Tuesday morning, taken a taxi to the house.

The house had been exactly as she remembered it.

This was, she thought as she stood on the small paved path in front of it with her small suitcase at her side, the first thing wrong. Houses that had sat empty for twelve years were not, in her limited experience of such houses, exactly as one remembered them. They were, in twelve years, sunken slightly. Their paint had faded. Their gardens had grown up around them in the specific patient way of Finnish gardens reclaiming Finnish houses. The house in front of her had, if anything, looked *more* itself than she had remembered — the white paint fresh, the small blue trim on the window frames bright, the small garden mown and edged, the birches in the front garden bare in the specific way of October birches that had been recently pruned.

She had thought, standing on the path: *father has been keeping this up.*

She had thought: *he has been keeping this up much more than he told me.*

She had, in a small unformed way, understood that this was not entirely surprising. Her father had, throughout her childhood, been a careful man. He had spent his working life as a small-town accountant, and had spent his private life keeping records of things. It was, in a way, consistent with him that he would, without mentioning it, have quietly maintained the house to a higher standard than the twice-yearly cleaning implied.

She had walked up to the door.

She had used the key her father had sent her. The key had turned in the lock without difficulty. The door had opened without the specific dry protest of a door long unused.

She had stepped inside.

—

The hallway had smelled like her childhood.

This too, she thought as she stood in the small hallway with the door closing behind her, was a wrongness. Houses that had been closed up for twelve years did not smell of her childhood. They smelled of dust, or of damp, or of the specific chemical bitterness of the cleaning products a semi-annual cleaner would have used. This house smelled of the particular soap her mother had used on the wooden floors, and of the small dried lavender her mother had kept in a bowl on the hall table, and — very faintly, almost imperceptibly — of the wool coats her mother had kept on the rack by the door.

There were no wool coats on the rack now. The rack was empty. But the smell of them was there, at the edge of the air, in the small trace way of a smell that had lingered because it had been recently there.

Sara stood in the hallway for a moment.

She had thought: *the cleaner uses the same soap. That is what it is. She uses the same soap and it smells the same.*

She had, as she thought this, understood that she was already, in her second minute in the house, offering herself explanations.

She had put her suitcase down. She had taken off her coat and hung it on the empty rack. She had walked, slowly, through the small ground floor of the house.

The sitting room had been as she remembered it. Her mother's small blue armchair, her father's larger green one, the small coffee table between them, the bookshelf along the north wall. The books on the shelf had been the same books. Her mother's small collection of Finnish poetry. Her father's small collection of history. There had been dust on the top shelf, in the specific thin way of dust that had settled over months rather than years.

The kitchen had been as she remembered it. The small round table where they had eaten breakfast. The four chairs. The small vase on the windowsill that had always held, in summer, some flower from the garden, and was now, in October, empty.

She had gone upstairs.

The upstairs of the house was two bedrooms and a small bathroom between them. Her own bedroom was on the left. Her parents' bedroom was on the right. The bathroom was in the middle.

She had gone into her own bedroom first.

Her bedroom had been as she had left it at eighteen. The small white iron bed. The desk under the window. The small framed print of a Kandinsky she had, at fifteen, considered the most sophisticated thing she owned. The desk drawer, when she opened it, had contained the small collection of pens and school supplies she had left behind when she had gone to Helsinki. The bookshelf had contained her childhood books.

She had, standing in the middle of her bedroom, thought: *he has kept everything.*

She had thought: *of course he has. Of course he has kept everything.*

She had turned to leave the bedroom, and had stopped, and had turned back, and had walked to the small chest of drawers under the window.

On the chest of drawers, in the small careful arrangement she had left when she was eighteen, were: her small silver hairbrush, her small wooden box of childhood jewelry, her small ceramic dish for the specific hairpins her mother had insisted she use to keep her fringe out of her eyes, and a small clean cotton handkerchief folded in a square.

She had picked up the handkerchief.

She had, she was certain, taken the handkerchief with her to Helsinki when she had left at eighteen. She remembered doing it. She remembered folding it into her small toiletry bag on the last morning, because it had been her grandmother's and had been embroidered by her grandmother with the initial S, and because she had wanted to have it in Helsinki with her.

The handkerchief on the chest of drawers had the small embroidered S in the corner in the same small careful cross-stitch.

She had stood with the handkerchief for a moment.

She had thought: *I brought it back for a visit. I brought it back on some visit and left it and forgot.*

She had put it back on the chest of drawers. She had walked out of her bedroom.

She had gone into the bathroom.

—

The bathroom had been small and white and exactly as she remembered it.

She had, without thinking, walked to the sink to wash her hands from the small dust of the journey. She had turned on the tap. The water had come. She had washed her hands with the small bar of white soap in the dish beside the sink, which she noted, and would later think about, was a fresh unused bar of the specific brand her mother had always used and had, throughout Sara's childhood, kept in the small dish beside this sink.

She had reached for the towel that had, throughout her childhood, hung on the rail by the door.

The towel had been there. It was fresh. It smelled clean, of the specific cheap detergent the cleaner presumably used, and it had, she saw as she dried her hands, been recently ironed.

She had dried her hands. She had turned to leave the bathroom.

She had, on her way to the door, glanced at the small shelf above the sink.

On the small shelf above the sink were three toothbrushes.

They were arranged in the small ceramic cup her mother had bought at a market in Helsinki when Sara was six. The cup had held, throughout her childhood, three toothbrushes. Her father's toothbrush had been the plain white one. Her mother's toothbrush had been the small pink one with the transparent handle. Sara's toothbrush had been the small green one with a picture of a cat on it, which had eventually been replaced, when she was nine, by a plain green one without the cat.

The three toothbrushes in the cup, on the small shelf above the sink, in the twelve-years-empty house, were: a plain white one, a small pink one with a transparent handle, and a plain green one.

The bristles of all three were slightly worn.

They had been, quite recently, used.

Sara had stood in the bathroom for a long time.

She had, at last, reached forward. She had picked up the plain green toothbrush. She had held it in her palm.

The bristles had been slightly damp.

—

She had left the bathroom.

She had walked, without hurry, downstairs. She had, in the sitting room, sat down on her mother's small blue armchair. She had sat with her hands in her lap. She had looked at the small coffee table.

There had been no dust on the small coffee table.

She had, sitting in her mother's armchair, thought carefully about several things.

She had thought, first, that there was a simple explanation for the toothbrushes. Her father was a careful man. He had, when he had asked her to come to the house, presumably prepared it. He had presumably driven up from Tampere in the previous week, and had presumably put out fresh soap and fresh towels, and had, in an excess of some emotion she could not immediately identify, replaced the three toothbrushes that had been in the small ceramic cup when her mother had died with three new ones of the same brands. This was, if slightly strange, not particularly frightening. It was the sort of thing a widowed accountant of seventy might do.

She had thought, second, that this explanation did not quite fit. The bristles of the toothbrushes had been slightly damp. Even if her father had put them out — say — the previous day, the bristles would have dried by Tuesday morning. Wet bristles suggested use within the last several hours. And Sara had, that morning, been the only person in the house.

She had thought, third, that there was a second, more disturbing explanation.

She had thought, fourth, that she was not, quite yet, going to permit herself to think it.

She had, sitting in the armchair, taken her phone from her pocket. She had, before she quite decided to, dialed her father's number.

The line had rung four times.

Her father's voice, when it had come, had been small and tired and, Sara thought immediately, distant. He had said: *Sara.*

She had said: *father. I am at the house.*

He had said: *good. Good, my girl. Is it — is it all right there?*

She had said: *it is very clean.*

He had said, after a pause: *yes. The cleaner comes twice a year, as I said.*

She had said: *father. Was anyone here recently?*

He had said: *what do you mean, my girl.*

She had said: *the — the bathroom is set up. There are toothbrushes. There is fresh soap. There is a fresh towel. There are three toothbrushes on the shelf above the sink.*

There had been a silence on the line.

Her father had said, after some seconds: *three.*

She had said: *yes. Father, three. One green. One pink. One white. Like when I was a child.*

Her father had said, very quietly: *my girl. I have not been to the house since your mother's funeral.*

He had said: *the cleaner comes twice a year, and she cleans, and she leaves. I have never asked her to prepare anything. I have never asked anyone to put toothbrushes on the shelf.*

He had said, more quietly: *I have not, my girl, ever gone in.*

Sara had sat in her mother's armchair with her phone against her ear, and she had understood, in the specific small clear way one understood things at the beginning of things, that whatever was in the house had not been put there by anyone she could name.

She had also understood, in the same small clear way, that whatever was in the house had known she was coming.

chapters.title: The Table Set for Three
chapters.body:
She stayed the first night.

She had thought about not staying. She had thought about going back to the small hotel near the market square, and about calling Ismo in Munich, and about explaining to him what she had found and asking him what she should do. She had thought about calling her father back and telling him that she was not, after all, going to do this — that he would need to hire someone, or send someone, or wait until he was well enough to come himself. She had thought about turning off the lights and locking the door and walking away.

She had done none of these things.

She had, instead, at six in the evening, walked down to the small grocery on the corner and had bought a loaf of bread and some cheese and a bottle of the specific cheap red wine that had, throughout her adolescence, been the wine her father had drunk on Friday evenings while listening to the radio. She had brought these things back to the house. She had put them on the small round kitchen table.

She had, then, gone upstairs and had unpacked her small suitcase in her own childhood bedroom, and had, without particular examination of what she was doing, taken off the clothes she had been wearing all day and put on the specific soft flannel pyjamas she had brought with her — pyjamas that she had, over the years in Munich, come to think of as her *home* pyjamas, the pyjamas she put on when she wanted, on a cold evening after a long day, to feel comfortable in the way one only felt comfortable in familiar clothing.

She had put on the pyjamas in her childhood bedroom, in her childhood house, on a cold October evening in Turku.

She had, when she had understood what she was doing, sat down on the small white iron bed and had held her face in her hands for perhaps a full minute.

Then she had gotten up. She had gone downstairs. She had opened the wine. She had cut the bread. She had cut the cheese. She had set a small plate for herself on the round kitchen table, and had sat down, and had eaten her small dinner in the specific small silence of a woman eating alone in a house that was too clean.

—

She had discovered the second thing after dinner.

She had, having finished eating, washed her plate and her glass at the sink, and had, on her way out of the kitchen, glanced at the small round table.

The table had four chairs. It had always had four chairs. Two long sides of the small square table, each with a chair, and two short sides, each with a chair. During Sara's childhood, when there had been three people in the house, the fourth chair had been kept as a spare, tucked in against the wall, and had been used only when guests had come.

The fourth chair, when she looked at it now, had been pulled out from the table.

It had been pulled out in the small definite way of a chair that had been sat in and had not been pushed back. It had been positioned at the short side of the table nearest the wall — the side that Sara herself, throughout her childhood, had sat at when she had eaten breakfast with her parents. The other three chairs had been in their ordinary positions.

She had not, that evening, moved the fourth chair. She had sat at the long side of the table, in her mother's usual seat, because it had felt correct to sit there. She had not touched the fourth chair.

She had stood in the doorway of the kitchen for a long time looking at it.

She had, at last, walked forward. She had, with the small definite motion of a woman doing something she had promised herself she was going to do without thinking about it, pushed the chair back into the table.

It had gone in easily. It had made no sound.

She had, without lingering, left the kitchen. She had turned off the light. She had gone into the sitting room.

She had sat down in her mother's armchair.

She had, sitting in her mother's armchair, become aware that she was being watched.

She had not been able to say, when she considered it afterwards, what particular feature of the sitting room had produced this sensation. There had been no one visible in the room. The lamps had been on. The curtains had been drawn, in the way her mother had always drawn them at dusk. The books on the shelves had been in their places. The small radio on the sideboard had been off. There had been, so far as her ordinary senses could determine, no reason to feel watched.

She had felt watched.

She had felt watched, more precisely, with the specific quality of a person who was watching her in *familiarity* — the way a parent might watch a grown child who had come home to visit, with the small quiet attention of someone who had known her for a long time and who wanted, on this rare visit, to look at her for a while.

Sara had sat in her mother's armchair.

She had, at last, said aloud, into the room: *hello.*

She had said it in Finnish. She had said it quietly. She had said it in the small careful way one might address a room in which one was uncertain there was anyone.

There had been no answer.

There had also been, she noticed, a small change in the room. The sense of being watched had, at the moment of her speaking, altered — had, she thought, *acknowledged* itself. It had, until she had spoken, been passive. It had, upon her speaking, become active. It had, in some small unspecifiable way, been focused on her.

She had, after a moment, said: *is someone here.*

She had, again, received no answer.

She had waited.

She had thought about what she had asked. She had thought about the specific formulation of the question. She had, in Finnish, asked *onko täällä joku*, which in Finnish was the ordinary way of asking whether someone was in a room, and which literally translated to *is there someone here.* She had thought about the possibility that the more specific question — *is my mother here, is my father here, is a stranger here* — would produce a more specific response.

She had, after another moment, said, aloud: *mother?*

The sense of being watched had, at the sound of the word, deepened.

Sara had sat very still in the armchair.

She had said, quietly: *mother, is that you?*

The sense of being watched had, at that second question, done something that she had not been able, on subsequent reflection, quite to describe. It had, she thought, *hesitated.* It had, in some way that had no ordinary equivalent, faltered — had, for a fraction of a second, become less certain of itself. Then it had settled again, at a slightly reduced intensity, in a specific position in the room that Sara could not have pointed to but that she felt to be, more or less, in the small space between her mother's armchair and the doorway.

She had understood, sitting in the armchair, several things.

She had understood that there was something in the house. She had understood that it was, so far as she could tell, aware of her. She had understood that it had responded, in some very small way, to her mother's name. She had understood that its response had not been an unambiguous *yes* — but had also not been an unambiguous *no*.

She had understood, above all, that it had been in the house for the twelve years since her mother had died.

She had understood, further, that it had been *waiting*.

—

She had, at last, gone to bed.

She had done this at eleven at night. She had, before going upstairs, walked once through every room of the ground floor and had turned off every light except a small lamp in the hallway. She had done this in the small careful way she had done it as a child, before she had gone up to bed on evenings when her parents had already gone up. It had been a small ritual her mother had taught her. *Check the taps,* her mother had said. *Check the stove. Check the doors.* Sara had, at eleven that night, checked the taps and the stove and the doors, in the same order she had checked them at twelve years old.

She had gone upstairs.

She had gone to the bathroom. She had, in front of the small mirror above the sink, brushed her teeth with a small travel toothbrush she had brought with her, from a small tube of travel toothpaste she had also brought. She had, when she had rinsed and spat, glanced up at the small ceramic cup on the shelf above the sink.

The three toothbrushes had been in the cup.

The plain green one had been slightly wet.

She had not, on that second time seeing them, permitted herself any particular reaction. She had returned her own toothbrush to the small toiletry bag in her hand. She had turned off the bathroom light. She had walked, along the small dark upstairs hallway, to her childhood bedroom.

She had, at the door of her childhood bedroom, paused.

She had looked, along the hallway, at the closed door of her parents' bedroom.

She had, throughout the whole of the day, not opened that door.

She had, without particular formal decision, understood that she was not going to open that door on the first night.

She had gone into her childhood bedroom. She had closed the door. She had, with a small deliberate motion, turned the small brass key in the lock, which she had used only once before in her life — at seventeen, on a specific evening when she had wanted her parents not to come in — and which she had, at eighteen, when she had left for Helsinki, left in the lock without particular thought.

The key had turned smoothly.

She had gotten into the small white iron bed.

She had turned off the small lamp beside the bed.

She had lain in the dark. She had listened to the specific small sounds of the house — the small creak of wood contracting in the cold, the small hum of the refrigerator downstairs, the small far-off sound of a car passing on the main road two streets over.

She had, at some point around midnight, heard a small sound in the hallway.

It had been the sound, unmistakably, of a footstep. A single small careful footstep on the wooden floor of the hallway, some distance from her door, in the direction of the bathroom.

There had been silence.

Then, after perhaps a minute, another small careful footstep.

Then, after another minute, the small sound of the bathroom door, which was always slightly stiff on its hinges, being opened.

Sara had lain very still.

She had listened.

She had heard, from the bathroom, the small definite sound of water running from a tap. She had heard the small sound of the tap being turned off. She had heard, more faintly, the small compressed sound of a small object being placed into a ceramic cup — the specific small sound of a toothbrush being returned to a stand.

She had heard the bathroom door close.

She had heard, again, the small careful footsteps, moving now away from the bathroom, along the hallway, toward the parents' bedroom.

She had heard, very faintly, the sound of that door opening.

She had heard it close.

Sara had lain in the dark in her childhood bedroom, in her childhood house, with the small brass key turned in the lock of her door, and she had, at last, cried quietly into her pillow — not with fear, though she was afraid, but with a specific quiet grief she had not felt in twelve years.

She had understood, lying in the dark, that her mother was in the house.

She had understood that her mother had been in the house for twelve years.

She had understood, further, and this had been the thing she had cried for, that her mother had been in the house *waiting.*

She had come home.

chapters.title: The Package
chapters.body:
She stayed for eight days.

She had not, when she had come, planned to stay eight days. She had planned to stay three or four — enough to sort through the immediate contents of the house, to make an inventory of what was there, to make preliminary contact with a real estate agent in the area, and then to fly back to Munich and to arrange the rest by correspondence over the following months. She had, on the first morning, thought about extending her stay to a week. By the third day she had understood that she was going to stay until she understood what she needed to do.

She did not, in the eight days, ever quite understand it.

She did, however, come to certain small decisions.

—

The first decision she came to was that she was not going to be afraid.

She came to this on the second morning. She had, after the first night, lain in bed for perhaps two hours after she had woken, watching the pale October light come slowly through the small window of her childhood bedroom. She had thought, during those two hours, about the small careful footsteps in the hallway. She had thought about the sound of the bathroom door. She had thought about the small compressed sound of the toothbrush being returned to the ceramic cup.

She had, at the end of the two hours, understood that whatever was in the house had not, at any point in the night, attempted to enter her locked bedroom. It had gone about its own small routine — brushing its teeth, using the bathroom, returning to the parents' bedroom — in the specific small way of a person who was going about her ordinary evening in her own ordinary house, and had, out of consideration or out of preference or out of some other reason Sara could not know, chosen not to disturb her sleeping daughter.

She had, on the third morning, unlocked her bedroom door.

She had left it unlocked from then on.

—

The second decision she came to was that she was not going to leave.

She came to this on the fourth day.

She had, on the fourth day, made herself go into the parents' bedroom.

She had done it in the late afternoon, in the specific soft light of the small window, at an hour she had chosen because it had been the hour her mother had always, in Sara's childhood, spent in the bedroom preparing for the evening. Her mother had had a small ritual. She had gone up to the bedroom around four in the afternoon, and had changed out of her working clothes, and had sat for perhaps twenty minutes on the small chair by the window doing what she called *thinking a little.* Sara had, in her childhood, sometimes come up and sat on the bed while her mother thought a little. They had not, on those visits, needed to speak.

Sara had, on the fourth afternoon of her return, opened the door to her parents' bedroom.

The room had been as she remembered it. The wide low bed with the pale linen coverlet. The small chair by the window. The chest of drawers along the north wall. The small oval mirror above it. The whole room had smelled, faintly, of the specific perfume her mother had worn — a small green Finnish perfume that had been made by a company that no longer existed, whose small square bottle had, throughout Sara's childhood, stood on the chest of drawers.

The small square bottle had been on the chest of drawers now.

Sara had walked, slowly, into the room. She had sat down on the small chair by the window.

She had, for a long moment, done nothing.

Then she had, quietly, said: *mother. I am here.*

There had been no answer. There had, however, been the same small quality of attention she had felt on the first evening in the sitting room — the small quiet feeling of being watched by someone who was watching her with familiarity. The feeling had, in the bedroom, been stronger. It had been, she thought, focused. It had been, she thought, sitting on the bed opposite her.

She had said, still quietly: *father is ill.*

She had said: *he has the same thing you had. He is not going to get better.*

She had said: *I have come to sort the house. He asked me to. He cannot come himself.*

She had, at these words, felt the attention shift very slightly. It had, she thought, softened. It had, she thought, been for a moment less on her and more on some quality of the room itself, some small internal recognition that was moving through it.

She had said: *I do not know what to do about you.*

She had said, more quietly: *I do not know what you want me to do.*

She had waited.

She had received, in the small quiet of the bedroom, no reply. But she had felt the attention, over the following minute, settle back on her. And she had understood, from the specific quality of it — the small familiar patience of it, the small careful readiness of it — that whatever her mother wanted from the house, and from Sara, was not something she was going to be able to name in words.

She had understood, sitting in the small chair by the window, that her mother wanted her *to know she was there.*

She had understood that this was the whole of it.

She had, sitting in the chair, begun to cry again — quietly, as she had cried on the first night, the small definite tears of a woman who had spent twelve years believing something was over and was now understanding that it had not been.

She had said, quietly: *I know you are here.*

She had said: *I know.*

She had said, and this had been the sentence she had not, throughout the whole of the last twelve years, been able to say to anyone: *I have missed you.*

The attention in the bedroom had, at this sentence, done something that Sara had felt in her whole body — a small warm settling, the specific sensation of being embraced by someone who was not present but who was, in some other way, near.

She had sat with it.

She had sat with it for a long time.

—

She had spent the following four days simply being in the house.

She had, over those four days, not done the work she had come to do. She had not sorted her mother's clothes. She had not made an inventory. She had not contacted the real estate agent. She had, instead, moved slowly through the house, in the way she had moved through it as a child, and had let her mother be with her.

Her mother had, over those four days, been present.

She had not, at any point, been visible. She had not, at any point, spoken. She had continued to use the bathroom at night — Sara had heard, on each of the following nights, the small careful footsteps and the small compressed sound of the toothbrush being returned — and had continued to occupy the parents' bedroom in the darker hours. But she had, during the days, been elsewhere in the house. She had been, Sara thought, wherever Sara was.

Sara had gotten used to this.

She had, by the seventh day, come to expect it. She had made her tea in the morning with the small quiet knowledge that her mother was in the kitchen with her. She had sat in the sitting room with her book in the afternoon with the small quiet knowledge that her mother was on the sofa opposite her. She had cooked her small dinners with the small quiet knowledge that her mother was watching, from her ordinary position at the counter, the way Sara chopped an onion or measured the salt.

She had spoken, occasionally. Small ordinary things. She had said, once: *this is not how you would do it.* She had said, once: *I am using too much butter.* She had said, once, quietly: *I do not know what I am doing here.*

Her mother had not responded in words. But the small quality of attention in the room had, at each thing Sara said, altered slightly — had, in the small way of a person listening with attention, acknowledged what had been said.

Sara had understood, over those four days, that she had been having, in her own way, a small quiet visit with her mother. She had been having the visit she had not had before her mother had died. She had been having it twelve years too late, in a small empty house that had, in some small mysterious way, held itself open for the visit.

She had understood that this was, in some form, a gift.

She had understood, further, that it was a gift that could not, by its nature, last very long.

—

On the eighth day the package arrived.

She had been in the kitchen. She had heard, at eleven in the morning, the small sound of the doorbell, which she had not heard in twelve years and which had sounded, when it came, exactly as she remembered it. She had walked to the front door.

The postman had been standing on the small paved path. He had been holding a small package, wrapped in brown paper, tied with string.

He had said: *for Aaltonen.*

She had said: *yes. That is me.*

He had held out the package. He had said: *no return address. Someone must have brought it to the office themselves.*

She had signed for the package. She had thanked him. She had, when he had gone, closed the door and stood in the hallway with the package in her hands.

The package had been small. It had been perhaps the size of a book. It had been wrapped in the specific brown paper her mother had used, throughout Sara's childhood, to wrap parcels. It had been tied with the specific white cotton string her mother had kept in a spool in the kitchen drawer.

On the front of the package, in her mother's small careful hand, had been written her own name and address:

*Sara Aaltonen*

The address below it had not been her current address in Munich. It had not been her father's address in Tampere. It had been the address of the small student flat she had lived in for two years after she had first left home, in Helsinki, when she had been eighteen and nineteen. It was an address she had not lived at in fifteen years.

The postmark on the package had been Turku, dated the previous week.

Sara had held the package in her hands for a long moment.

She had walked into the sitting room. She had sat down in her mother's armchair. She had, slowly, untied the string.

She had opened the paper.

Inside the paper had been a small book. It had been a small handmade book, sewn together with the specific white thread her mother had used for sewing on buttons. Its cover had been a small piece of pale blue cardboard. On the cover, in her mother's small careful hand, had been written:

*For Sara. To read when you come home.*

Sara had opened the book.

The pages had been in her mother's handwriting. They had been dated. The first entry had been from twelve years ago — from the last month of her mother's life. The last entry had been from the previous week.

Her mother had, for twelve years, been keeping a journal.

Her mother had, for twelve years, been writing to her, quietly, in the empty house, in the small careful hand of a woman who had known she would not be answered, who had known she would perhaps never be read, and who had, all the same, kept writing.

Sara had read the first entry.

*My Sara,*

*I do not know if I will be able to say all of this before I go. So I am writing it, instead, for you. I am writing this from my chair by the bedroom window. It is October. The light is going. I am writing because I have understood, over the last month, that I am going to die soon, and that there are certain things I want you to know that I have not been able to say to you in person. I have not been able to say them because they are small things, and because our family is a family of small things unsaid, and because I have understood too late that these are, in the end, the only things that matter.*

*I want you to know that I have loved you well.*

*I have not always been able to show this. I have been a small careful woman in a small careful marriage in a small careful house in a small careful country, and I have not always known how to show what I felt. But I have loved you, from the first afternoon I held you in the hospital in Turku when the light through the window was the same soft grey it is now, and I have loved you every day since, and I love you now, and I will love you after.*

*If I have anything to give you at the end, it is this.*

*Your mother.*

Sara had read the entry twice.

She had turned the page.

—

She had read the whole book on the eighth day.

She had read it slowly, in her mother's armchair, over the course of that afternoon and evening. She had, over the course of it, understood what her mother had been doing in the house for twelve years. Her mother had been writing. She had been writing entries at intervals of a few weeks. She had been writing about the small ordinary things she saw and heard in the house. She had been writing about the light in the sitting room in December. She had been writing about a small green wren that had made a nest under the eaves the second summer after her death. She had been writing about the specific quiet loneliness of a woman who had continued to exist in her own house after her death, and who had not known why she continued, and who had, over the years, come to accept that she continued because she was waiting for something.

The something had been Sara.

Her mother had, in the last entry, dated the previous week, written:

*My Sara,*

*Your father telephoned this evening. He does not, of course, know that I hear him. But I hear him when he calls the house — I have understood over the years that if I am in the house when the telephone rings, I can, without picking it up, hear whatever is said on the other end. He does not call often. Tonight he called to leave a message on the answering machine, which he does when he has thought about something for a long time and wants, I think, to say it out loud into the empty house. He said that he has been ill. He said that he has been diagnosed with the illness that took me. He said that he has asked you to come to the house.*

*He said that you have said yes.*

*I have, on hearing this, understood two things.*

*The first is that I will not have to wait very much longer.*

*The second is that this journal, which I have kept for twelve years without a purpose, has had, all along, a purpose. It has been for the day you would come. It has been so that you would know I have been here. It has been so that you would know I have been thinking of you.*

*I do not know, my Sara, what will happen when you arrive. I do not know whether you will feel me. I do not know whether I will be able, in the end, to make my presence known to you at all. It is possible that you will come and go and never know I was here. That would be all right. I have not, in twelve years, been unhappy. I have been quiet. I have been patient. I have, above all, been waiting for you.*

*Come when you can, my daughter.*

*I will be here.*

*Your mother.*

Sara had closed the small book.

She had sat with it for a long time.

She had understood, sitting in her mother's armchair on the evening of the eighth day, several things.

She had understood that her mother had, throughout the eight days, been able to feel her presence. She had understood that her mother had been, in her own small way, glad. She had understood that the small package on the doormat had not been sent from any post office — that her mother had, in some way, arranged for it to arrive on the day Sara would be ready to read it.

She had understood, further, that this was the end.

She had understood this without needing to be told. She had understood it from the small settled quality of the last journal entry. She had understood it from the small careful arrangement of the package. She had understood, above all, from the small quality of attention in the sitting room, which had, over the course of the afternoon, become slowly quieter — had begun, she thought, in the specific way of a person who had finished what she had come to say, to *lift.*

She had put the small book down on the coffee table.

She had said, quietly, into the room: *thank you.*

She had said: *I have read it. I have read all of it.*

She had said: *I love you.*

The small quality of attention in the sitting room had, for one last moment, settled fully on her — had, in that last moment, been the closest she had ever felt to being held by her mother — and had then, slowly, in the small way of a warm hand lifting from a shoulder, gone.

The house had, at that moment, become an ordinary empty house.

Sara had sat in her mother's armchair for a long time.

Then she had gotten up. She had gone into the kitchen. She had made herself a cup of tea. She had drunk it slowly at the small round table, at her own childhood seat, in the small quiet of a house that was, now, only a house.

—

She had flown back to Munich on the ninth day.

She had, before she had left, made two small changes to the house. She had removed the two extra toothbrushes from the ceramic cup and had wrapped them in a small piece of tissue paper and had put them in the pocket of her suitcase. She had taken the small square bottle of her mother's perfume from the chest of drawers in the parents' bedroom and had done the same.

She had, otherwise, left everything as it was.

She had, on the taxi ride back to the airport, telephoned her father. She had told him that she had spent a week in the house. She had told him that she had begun the process of sorting things and that she would come back in a few weeks to continue. She had not, on the telephone, told him about her mother. She had understood, on the eighth evening, that this was the part of the story that was hers alone.

She had, later, when her father had died — some four months after Sara's visit, quietly, in his apartment in Tampere — arranged for him to be buried next to her mother in the small cemetery in Turku. She had, at the funeral, said nothing to anyone about the house. She had, on the following morning, gone to the house one last time.

She had walked through it slowly, in the pale March light. She had sat, for a long moment, in her mother's armchair. She had gone up to the parents' bedroom, and had sat in the small chair by the window, and had said, quietly: *he is with you now.*

The house had not answered.

She had, on the way out, put the small handmade blue book on the small table by the door.

She had locked the front door behind her, and had, that afternoon, met with the real estate agent. The house had sold, within three weeks, to a young family with two small children who had wanted, they had said in the small careful way of young families in Finland, a house with a good garden and a quiet street.

Sara had not, at any point, gone back.

She had lived, from then on, in Munich, with Ismo, and had, over the years, had two children of her own, and had, at fifty-two, come to be a small quiet careful mother in her own small quiet careful house in a suburb of Munich, and had, over the years, not spoken to her children about her own mother in any detail beyond the small ordinary details of a life.

She had, however, kept the small blue book.

She had kept it in the top drawer of her own desk. She had read it, from time to time, in the quiet hours of her own middle age, when her children were at school and her house was empty. She had read it slowly. She had, each time, understood something new.

She had understood, most often, this:

That love was a thing that continued.

That it continued in ways that were not always known to the person who continued it.

That it continued, sometimes, in a small empty house on a small quiet street, for twelve years, waiting.

That someone must always, in the end, come home.
